newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Dismissed Lebed predicts "hot autumn" in Russia.
newsitem.headline: Dismissed Lebed predicts "hot autumn" in Russia.

text.p: Sacked Russian security chief Alexander Lebed called on his supporters to stay calm in the wake of his dismissal by President Boris Yeltsin on Thursday but he warned of a "hot autumn" to come.
"I call on my comrades in arms, my allies and people who I probably do not know in person...do not do anything abrupt. We act only using constitutional means," he told a news conference.

Lebed was speaking less than three hours after Yeltsin appeared on national television, accused him of lack of team spirit and open ambition to become the country's next leader and signed a decree dismissing him.
He said he was not surprised that his marriage of convenience with Yeltsin's team had collapsed.
"I was a black sheep in the herd," said the paratroop general, renowned for his lack of respect towards the Kremlin. "It was only a matter of time before they sacked me. I am not part of their herd."

Lebed joined Yeltsin's administration after coming third with 11 million votes in June in the first round of presidential elections. The transfer was crucial in helping the president to overcome the challenge of communist rival Gennady Zyuganov.
Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov accused Lebed on Wednesday of trying to seize power in Russia by force. Lebed denied the accusation, but confirmed he planned to seek the presidency.
"Firstly I plan to have a good sleep...Then I will start polishing (my) political machine to be ready for the presidential election," he said.
He denied that he was in a hurry, saying: "I am not going to launch pre-election campaign while the president is alive." Yeltsin has accused Lebed and other rivals of doing just that.
Lebed, named in a recent opinion poll as Russia's most trusted politician, was ambiguous when asked what he would do if his supporters held protests against his dismissal.
"I want to see first whether this will happen. I will make my decisions judging by the circumstances," he replied.
But, predicting that a severe lack of funding for the armed forces would provoke a crisis later this year, he said: "We are heading for a very hot autumn, no doubt about it."
To back his claim, he cited a letter from a group of General Staff officers in which they told the Defence Ministry to pay all salary arrears by October 25 or face the consequences.
"I think this (crisis) will start on October 25, as can be seen from the letter," Lebed told his news conference, which was organised by Interfax news agency.

The letter, addressed to Defence Minister Igor Rodionov and published by the Nezavisimaya Gazeta newspaper, said keeping the armed forces "half-starved" was a deliberate act by sinister forces who wanted to ruin Russia and surrender it to the West.
"We have enough force to make these gentlemen abandon their plans," it said. The newspaper did not say how many officers had signed it.

Lebed, who signed an August peace deal with separatist rebels to end 21 months of fighting in Chechnya, also said his departure could upset prospects for peace in the region. "I think the impact will be pretty negative," he said.

He implied that his inquiry into responsibility for the Chechen conflict had played a key role in his sacking. "The main reason is that two days ago I sent to the president results of my investigation into who was to blame for Chechnya," he said.
